facts.quote: The default docker-compose.yml includes the AI Gateway (beta) as the langfuse-ai-gateway service, listening on port 3031.

caveats: Chạy trực tiếp bằng Node mà không qua Docker yêu cầu phiên bản rất mới là Node.js 24.22.3 trở lên.
Nếu máy chủ không cài Docker, AI agent sẽ không có môi trường sandbox shell độc lập mà chỉ có quyền đọc/ghi file.
Chế độ kết nối điều khiển thực thi từ xa (remote execution) hiện vẫn đang ở bản phát triển, yêu cầu server và Python connector phải dùng chung một bản mã nguồn được kiểm duyệt (checkout).

Dung lượng các tệp học tập bị giới hạn tuyệt đối (2048 bytes cho corrections.md, 16384 bytes cho workflow draft); vượt quá giới hạn hoặc dính định dạng secret sẽ bị hệ thống từ chối lưu thay vì cắt ngắn nội dung.
Bật tính năng tự cải tiến (self-improving) sẽ làm phát sinh thêm chi phí token vì server phải thực hiện tác vụ phản tư (reflection) và chấm điểm độc lập (independent grading).
Langfuse thuần về tracing/observability qua OpenTelemetry và không hỗ trợ cơ chế phục hồi tiến trình bị gián đoạn hay tự động tạo workflow như AgentRun.
gaps: Mức tiêu hao tài nguyên phần cứng thực tế (RAM và CPU tối thiểu) khi chạy một instance AgentRun kèm Docker sandbox trên VPS giá rẻ.
AgentRun có hỗ trợ xuất trực tiếp telemetry qua OTLP sang Langfuse để tận dụng cả hai công cụ cùng lúc hay không.
Cách cấu hình Reverse Proxy (như Nginx/Caddy) kèm HTTPS và chứng chỉ SSL cho AgentRun trên VPS mà không dùng Tailscale.
Khả năng phân quyền người dùng (multi-tenant/RBAC) trên bảng điều khiển tự host của AgentRun.

## Parcha-ai/agentrun (https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun)
Description: AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer tokens with every run.
Homepage: https://agentrun.ai
Language: JavaScript; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-09-23; last push 2026-11-18
Latest release: cli-v0.1.10 (2026-11-06)
README (start):
Run smarter agents. Use fewer tokens.

  Our code review bill went up 36x this year. Now a review costs us 18 cents. See how ↓

  
  
  
  

  AgentRun Cloud ·
  Run locally ·
  Self-host

  Quickstart ·
  Connect your agent ·
  Case studies ·
  Tour ·
  Templates ·
  Deploy ·
  Docs

AgentRun is an open-source platform that supercharges your agents. It adds self-improvement, durable execution and a
control plane on top of your favorite agent harness. Your agents become smarter, more fault tolerant and use fewer
tokens with every run.

  
  An agent's Learning tab: what it kept, and what changed since. Demo data from the console's recorded fixtures.

## Case studies

  
  

**Code review.** Greptile started charging a dollar a review in March, then our agents took off, and our bill went
from $180 a month to $6,451. So we built our own reviewer on a cheap model and tuned it on our own PRs. It costs 18 cents a review, and on 30 PRs
it had never seen it caught 1.6x the real bugs Greptile did. [How we built it](docs/case-studies/code-review.md) · [Tune one on your repo](docs/tutorials/tune-a-template.md)

**Merchant codes.** We let Opus figure out how to classify merchants, then handed what it learned to a cheap model.
Same job, $0.89 down to $0.12 a merchant. [How it works](docs/case-studies/merchant-classification.md) · [Do it with your own job](docs/tutorials/learn-then-hand-off.md)

## Why AgentRun

Agents are great at figuring things out. The problem is they figure out the same things over and over. Give an agent
a job it has done a hundred times and it rediscovers the same API, rereads the same docs and rebuilds the same plan, and
you pay for every token of it.

Bring your agent on the harness it runs best on: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or pi. AgentRun does everything around it:

- **It learns the work.** After each run, the agent keeps what will help next time: a note, a skill, or a workflow
  that does the job without the loop. The next run starts from there.
- **It never loses a run.** Every run lives in one store. Kill the server mid-run, start it again, and the run carries
  on. Give each agent the computer the job needs: a sandbox, a Linux desktop, an Android phone or a browser.
- **You stay in control.** Approvals, spend caps and one console for every agent: what needs you, what failed, what's
  running and what it cost.

You don't build the plumbing: provider integrations, recovery, run tracking and learning are all here. Use
[AgentRun Cloud](docs/getting-started.md#agentrun-cloud) for hosted access, or run the open-source platform on your
laptop, in one container, or as a server with runners. Apache-2.0.

## Get started

**AgentRun Cloud.** Run agents without maintaining your own server. [Open Cloud](https://console.agentrun.ai/) to
create an account or sign in. For help setting up your team's workflows,
[talk to us](https://calendly.com/d/dtwn-dsp-nx5/agentrun).

Prefer your own machine or infrastructure? Start locally below, or [self-host on Railway, Render, a VPS or Docker](#deploy-it).
The [getting-started guide](docs/getting-started.md) explains the three options.

### Run locally in three steps

You need Node 24.22.3 or newer, on macOS or Linux.

Already use Claude Code or Codex? [Connect your existing agent](#connect-your-existing-agent) with its current
configuration and sign-in. You do not need to add a model key to AgentRun for that connection. The steps below
start a new agent from a template.

1. **Start it.**

   ```sh
   npx @parcha/agentrun
   ```

   It starts the server and one runner on port 7340 (or the next free one), keeps everything in `~/.agentrun`, and
   opens the console in your browser.

2. **Continue with ChatGPT, or add a model key.** In the console, set a password, then press **Continue with ChatGPT**
   (on the first screen, or under **Settings → Model keys**) and sign in on OpenAI's page: Codex and pi agents run on
   your ChatGPT plan, with no key. Or add a key in the same place: one `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` gives every harness a model;
   an Anthropic key runs pi and Claude Code; an OpenAI key runs pi, Codex and OpenCode.

3. **Run your first agent.** Open **Templates**, apply **KYB due diligence**, and start a run with a company's name and
   website. It needs nothing but your ChatGPT sign-in or your model key. When it finishes, the run's **Report** tab has
   a due diligence report with a verdict and every claim cited. Then open the agent's **Learning** tab to see what it
   kept for next time.

Rather have your coding agent do it? Tell it `Read https://agentrun.ai/SKILL.md and set up AgentRun for me`.
That page is [the setup skill](docs/SKILL.md) in this repository: it asks where AgentRun should run (this computer,
your own always-on machine, Railway, Render or AgentRun Cloud) before it installs anything. It brings in a Claude Code
or Codex job you already schedule as the first run, or creates and runs a first agent with you.

Docker, sandboxes and running it on a server

If Docker is running on your machine, new agents get a Docker sandbox with a shell. Its image builds on first use,
which takes a few minutes, and the console says when it's ready. Without Docker, agents still read and write files,
but get no shell.

Want your own server with a URL? [Self-host on Railway or Render](#deploy-it).

## Connect your existing agent

Already have agents running in a backend, Docker deployment or terminal? **Connect agent** can observe them
through the same CLI and OpenTelemetry Collector used by hosted AgentRun. The OSS console shows their reported
activity and token usage while your application keeps starting the work. Follow
[Observe agents that already run elsewhere](connector/README.md#observe-agents-that-already-run-elsewhere).
Observation needs no model key and does not automatically enable learning or import transcripts.

Keep the project, instructions, skills, MCP tools and sign-in you already use in Claude Code or Codex. AgentRun can
start new jobs with that setup and show their activity and results in the console.

**Development build:** remote connections currently require the server and the Python connector from the same
reviewed checkout. The published observation-only CLI does not include this remote execution mode. Follow the
[source connector setup](connector/README.md) for installation and the matching Node bridge.

1. **Choose your coding agent.** In Mission Control or Connected agents, open the **Connect agent** dropdown and
   select your coding agent. The button remembers your choice and provides a prompt that reads the skill from
   this server's build.
2. **Choose what to bring.** The skill first distinguishes **observing existing sessions** from letting AgentRun
   **start future jobs**. For future jobs, choose **a live connection**, **past history**, or **both**,
   then confirms the source machine, project and runtime. For a laptop, VM or container separate from the server,
   use **Connection setup → Another machine** and create a code with the chosen scope. Enter it directly in the
   source CLI's secure prompt. Your native credentials stay on that machine; the worker connects outbound.
3. **See the result.** For **History only**, open Runs and check the imported conversations and counts; no worker
   or model job is started. For a **live connection** or **Both**, open the connected agent, verify its setup, and
   start a job. Keep a remote source worker online. Optionally turn **Self-improving** On to let completed jobs
   propose notes and skills. Inspect what passes checking and grading in Learning Dojo, then start a fresh run to
   use it. Reflection and grading add model usage.

History import brings selected completed conversations into Runs without executing them or automatically training
the agent. A live connection starts new CLI sessions; it does not attach to a desktop conversation already in
progress. You can connect first and import history later with an explicitly approved history scope.

[Connection and history guide](docs/native-agents.md) · [Remote CLI installation and commands](connector/README.md)

Already run an agent inside your backend with an SDK? The development build can add checked learning around its
existing call site. Your backend keeps its job queue, tools, model credentials and cancellation; AgentRun records
the run and supplies accepted learning to the next fresh task. Use the matching client and server from this checkout.

| Backend SDK | Integration |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Agent SDK | [Wrap your existing query and custom tools](docs/tutorials/claude-sdk-learning.md) |
| Codex SDK | [Wrap your existing Codex client and fresh threads](docs/tutorials/codex-sdk-learning.md) |

The [live examples](examples/sdk-learning/README.md) verify native tool execution, an accepted note or skill, fresh-run reuse,
and a learning-Off control. Reflection and independent grading run on the server and add model usage.

## Take the tour

**Workflows that make the call.** A step can ask a fast typed question, see how sure the answer is, and pick a route.
Here the model leans approve at 0.61, below the workflow's 0.75 bar, so the case goes to review.

  

**Every agent in one place.** Mission Control opens first: what needs you, what failed, what's running and what it
cost, by day, by harness and by tool.

  

**Every agent is an API.** Start a run from the Playground, then copy the same request into your code.

  

**You stay in control.** An agent can stop and ask you, and the run waits until you answer.

  

## Agents that learn the work

Turn it on with `"learning": true` in an agent's definition. An agent learns two things, both kept in its own git
folder, and every run starts from that folder's `main`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    start["Run starts fromthe agent's main"] --> work["Run does the job"]
    work --> fin["Run's end: your words to corrections.md,a workflow draft when one is due"]
    fin --> check["Code checks,then one replay check"]
    check -->|kept| commit["Commit to main"]
    commit --> start
```

- **Corrections** are your words. A grade's words, or a message you send after a run's first answer, become one line
  of the agent's `corrections.md` at that run's end. Every later run is given the file whole, under `# Learned`.
- **Learned workflows** run as one tool call on any harness, under the run's own cap and tool permissions. Once the
  agent has 20 completed runs (`learning: { "compile_after": 20 }` is the default), one run's end compiles the job into
  a workflow draft. Code checks the draft and dry-runs it (no model is asked and no tool runs), then it is replayed
  once on those runs' inputs and serves only when it answers enough of them alone and agrees with the agent's answers.

The agent's **Learning** tab shows its corrections, its workflows and the log of changes. Edit the corrections there,
or with `PUT /v2/agents/{id}/learning/corrections`. Git keeps the history.

What gets kept, and what gets refused

Each agent has a learning folder: plain git with one branch, `main`. Over a cap a write is refused whole, never cut:
2048 bytes for `corrections.md`, 16384 for a draft's `workflow.json`, 1024 for its README. A secret or a secret's
shape in a correction or a draft refuses it too. A held draft gets one revision, shown the inputs it disagreed on;
held again, it stops, and nothing compiles again until you act.

## Workflows

A lot of agents don't need to be agents. Write repeatable work as a typed workflow: tool calls, model steps and fast
typed decisions (yes or no, pick one, a score, each with its confidence), with an agent to fall back on when a case is
unclear. AgentRun runs it as an agent's revision, under the agent's tool permissions and a cap like any run, and a
trigger can start one.

  
  An illustration of the control flow in examples/support-answer.mjs, not a recording of a model run.

## langfuse/langfuse (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse)
Description: 🪢 Open source AI engineering platform: AI Gateway, agent observability, evals, and prompt/skill management, built on OpenTelemetry. One open platform for every AI call and every agent. Self-host or use Langfuse Cloud.
Homepage: https://langfuse.com
Language: TypeScript; license: NOASSERTION; created 2023-05-18; last push 2026-11-18
Latest release: v4.82.0 (2026-11-17)
README (start):
Langfuse Cloud
          · 
         
            Self-Host
          · 
         
            Demo

Langfuse is an **open source AI engineering platform** for **agent evals and observability**. It is one open platform for every AI call your company makes and every agent your teams build: track usage and costs, **trace and evaluate** agents, and use production data to ship better AI. Use Langfuse Cloud or **self-host in minutes**; Langfuse is **battle-tested** at scale.

Watch a quick demo of the project here:

> ### 🧑‍💻 We're hiring
>
> Interested in contributing to Langfuse full-time? Langfuse is growing fast (we doubled the team in the last 6 months). Since January 2026 we're part of ClickHouse. We hire remotely, with offices in Berlin, San Francisco, Amsterdam, and New York.
> **[See open roles →](https://langfuse.com/careers?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=hiring&utm_content=langfuse)**

## ✨ Core Features

- [AI Observability](https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/overview): Instrument your app and start ingesting traces to Langfuse, thereby tracking LLM calls and other relevant logic in your app such as retrieval, embedding, or agent actions. Inspect and debug complex logs and user sessions. Built on OpenTelemetry. Try the interactive [demo](https://langfuse.com/docs/demo) to see this in action.

- [Prompt Management](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/overview) helps you centrally manage, version control, and collaboratively iterate on your prompts. Thanks to strong caching on server and client side, you can iterate on prompts without adding latency to your application. The [LLM Playground](https://langfuse.com/docs/prompt-management/features/playground) lets you test prompts and model configurations; when you see a bad result in tracing, you can jump straight to the playground to iterate on it.

- [Skill Management](https://langfuse.com/docs/skill-management/overview) (beta) brings versioning and labels to agent skills: a `SKILL.md` with task instructions plus optional supporting files. Promote or roll back versions without changing application code, and link skill versions to the traces they produced.

- [Evaluations](https://langfuse.com/docs/evaluation/overview) are key to the AI agent development workflow, and Langfuse adapts to your needs. It supports LLM-as-a-judge, code evaluators, user feedback collection, manual labeling, and custom evaluation pipelines via APIs/SDKs. Use [Datasets and Experiments](https://langfuse.com/docs/evaluation/experiments/datasets) to build test sets and benchmarks for pre-deployment testing and continuous improvement.

- [AI Gateway](https://langfuse.com/docs/gateway/overview) (beta) gives your organization one endpoint for calls to your model providers. Keep provider credentials in one place, hand out per-user or service account gateway keys, approve models centrally, track AI spend per user, key, and model, and record every call as a Langfuse trace.

- [Metrics and Dashboards](https://langfuse.com/docs/metrics/overview): Track latency, cost, and quality across any dimension with [custom dashboards](https://langfuse.com/docs/metrics/features/custom-dashboards), the metrics API, and alerts.

- [Comprehensive API](https://langfuse.com/docs/api-and-data-platform/overview): Langfuse is frequently used to power bespoke AI engineering workflows while using the building blocks provided by Langfuse via the API. An OpenAPI spec, typed SDKs for Python and JS/TS, the [Langfuse CLI](https://langfuse.com/docs/api-and-data-platform/features/cli), and the [Langfuse Agent Skill](https://langfuse.com/docs/api-and-data-platform/features/agent-skill) for coding agents are available.

## 📦 Deploy Langfuse

### Langfuse Cloud

Managed deployment by the Langfuse team, generous free tier, no credit card required.

**[Sign up for Langfuse Cloud →](https://langfuse.com/cloud)**

### Self-Host Langfuse

Run Langfuse on your own infrastructure:

- [Docker Compose](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/docker-compose): Run Langfuse on your own machine or a single virtual machine in 5 minutes. The guide also covers configuring Docker log rotation so container logs don't fill up the disk.

  ```bash
  # Get a copy of the latest Langfuse repository
  git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git
  cd langfuse

  # Run the langfuse docker compose
  docker compose up
  ```

- [Kubernetes (Helm)](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/kubernetes-helm): Run Langfuse on a Kubernetes cluster using Helm. This is the preferred production deployment.
- Terraform Templates: [AWS](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/aws), [Azure](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/azure), [GCP](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/gcp)
- Community-maintained: [Render](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/render), [Railway](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting/deployment/railway)

See [self-hosting documentation](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting) to learn more about architecture and configuration options.

> [!TIP]
> **Self-hosting Langfuse?** Subscribe to the [self-hosting update list](https://langfuse.com/self-hosting#subscribe) to get an email about important features and new releases for open source Langfuse — self-hosting updates only, no marketing.

## 🔌 Integrations

Langfuse is built on [OpenTelemetry](https://langfuse.com/integrations/native/opentelemetry), so any OpenTelemetry-instrumented application, framework, or collector can send traces to Langfuse.

### Main Integrations

| Integration                                                                     | Supports                       | Description                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [OpenTelemetry](https://langfuse.com/integrations/native/opentelemetry)         | Any language                   | Send OTLP traces from your application or OpenTelemetry Collector to Langfuse's OpenTelemetry endpoint.                                          |
| [Langfuse AI Gateway](https://langfuse.com/docs/gateway/overview) (beta)        | Any OpenAI or Anthropic client | Route model calls through one endpoint to trace every call, keep provider keys in one place, and track cost without SDK or code changes.         |
| [SDK](https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/sdk/overview)                     | Python, JS/TS                  | Manual instrumentation using the SDKs for full flexibility.                                                                                      |
| [OpenAI](https://langfuse.com/integrations/model-providers/openai-py)           | Python, JS/TS                  | Automated instrumentation using drop-in replacement of OpenAI SDK.                                                                               |
| [LangChain & LangGraph](https://langfuse.com/integrations/frameworks/langchain) | Python, JS/TS                  | Automated instrumentation by passing callback handler to LangChain or LangGraph application.                                                     |
| [LlamaIndex](https://langfuse.com/integrations/frameworks/llamaindex)           | Python                         | Automated instrumentation via LlamaIndex callback system.                                                                                        |
| [Haystack](https://langfuse.com/integrations/frameworks/haystack)               | Python                         | Automated instrumentation via Haystack content tracing system.                                                                                   |

# Open-source framework for workflow orchestration in your product

### Your users draw the workflow. Temporal runs it. You see every step.

Workflow Builder ships the full stack: a white-label React workflow builder for your users, durable execution on your own [Temporal](https://temporal.io), human approval steps for AI agents and business processes, and a live view of every run.

[](https://github.com/synergycodes/workflowbuilder/actions/workflows/build.yml)
[](./LICENSE)
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@workflowbuilder/sdk)
[](https://discord.com/invite/FDMjRuarFb)

**[▶ Run a workflow in your browser](https://aistudio.workflowbuilder.io/)** · no install, no sign-up

[Embed the editor](#path-a-embed-the-sdk) · [Orchestrate on your Temporal](#path-d-add-workflow-orchestration-on-your-temporal) · [Run the full stack](#path-c-run-the-full-stack-demo) · [Documentation](https://www.workflowbuilder.io/docs/overview/)

## Drawing boxes and arrows is the easy part

Your customers want to automate their work inside your product, not in another tool. With React Flow and an AI assistant, a demo canvas takes a weekend. The time goes into everything around it:

- **An editor people can work in all day:** forms generated from your schemas, validation, your node types, your design system.
- **Durability:** a run picks up where it left off after a crash or a worker restart, retries the flaky step and fails fast on the broken one.
- **Human-in-the-loop:** a step waits for a person to approve, correct or reject, for minutes or for weeks, with nothing polling in the meantime.
- **Versions:** your customers run the published version while they edit the next one, and every run is pinned to the graph it started with.
- **A live view of every run:** what ran, what it returned, where it waits, why it failed.

Workflow Builder ships all of it, the editor and the workflow orchestration on Temporal behind it, as one open-source stack on your infrastructure. Use the whole stack, or only the parts you need.

## What you get

**Build.** A complete workflow editor in your React app: palette, canvas and a properties panel generated from JSON Schema, with validation. Your node types, your design tokens and logo, light and dark themes, plugins. Workflows are saved as JSON to your API, a callback or `localStorage`. [Vercom](https://www.workflowbuilder.io/case-study/vercom), [Athena Intelligence](https://www.workflowbuilder.io/case-study/athena-intelligence) and [Plura AI](https://www.workflowbuilder.io/case-study/plura-ai) built their workflow editors on it.

**Orchestrate.** Durable workflow orchestration on your own Temporal, self-hosted or [Temporal Cloud](https://temporal.io/cloud): the diagrams your users draw run as durable workflows. One generic workflow runs any diagram with one start node and no loops, so a new or changed process ships without new workflow code, as long as it uses node types your Workers already run. Independent branches run in parallel and join, a decision routes the run down one branch, each node type can get its own timeout and retry cap, and an error that cannot succeed on retry fails fast instead of burning attempts.

**Decide.** Pause any step for a person. The run waits in Temporal, for minutes or for weeks, holding no Worker and running no code, until someone approves, approves with corrections, or rejects with a reason. The first decision wins, a late one is refused with an answer, and the decision, corrections included, is recorded with the run for the next steps to read.

**Observe.** Watch a run live on the canvas: each step is marked running, completed, failed, skipped or waiting, and the log shows what every step returned and why one failed. Every run keeps the exact graph it ran and its ordered event history, streamed to the browser as it happens. In Temporal Web UI each step shows up under your node's name. AI Studio has this run view built in, as open code you can carry into your own app.

**Own.** Apache 2.0, the whole stack in this repository: embed it, white-label it, ship it to your customers. It runs on your Temporal and your Postgres, with any OpenAI-compatible model, including one inside your network. No per-run pricing from us, and open code you can fork.

## How it fits together

**Editor SDK · Temporal Plugin · Execution backend: open code, yours to own.**

# Set up AgentRun

AgentRun is an open-source platform for running agents: a console in the browser, runs that survive a restart, a
spend cap on every run, and agents that learn from their own runs. Get the person from this prompt to a finished first
run in about five minutes, with no Node install, no Terminal steps and no hunt for a key. Never ask for a password, key
or token in this chat, never print one, and never put one on a command line.

## How to ask

Ask every choice in this setup with your host's question tool. Call the tool; don't write the choices as chat text.
Loading the tool and then asking in prose anyway is the mistake to avoid.

- Claude Code: `AskUserQuestion`. If it is listed but not loaded yet, load it, then call it.
- Codex: `request_user_input` (Plan mode). In Default mode it isn't available: ask one short plain question that
  names the answer you recommend.
- Cursor: `AskQuestion` ("Ask questions"). OpenCode: `question`.
- pi: `question` or `questionnaire` if an extension added one. Otherwise use the fallback.
- Any other host: its own ask tool (Gemini CLI and Copilot: `ask_user`; Hermes: `clarify`).

Each question is one sentence with a header of 12 characters or less and 2 or 3 options. Each option has a label of
1-5 words and a one-line description that states the cost or what happens. Put the option you recommend first and end
its label with "(Recommended)". Don't add an "Other" or "Skip" option; the tool adds a free-text answer. Ask one
question per call. Put two questions in one call only when neither answer changes the other.

After you ask, stop and wait. Don't start the step while the question is open. If the answer is free text, map it to
an option; if it doesn't match one, answer it and ask again.

No question tool, or the call fails: send the same question as one short message, options numbered, recommended
first, and end with "Reply with a number." Then stop. A reply that doesn't pick an option is not a yes for anything
that installs, deploys or spends. Never answer a question for the person, and never pass a flag that answers one.

## 1. Look at this session

Before asking anything, run this. It only reads, and prints the names of the signals it finds, never their values:

```sh
uname -s
for name in CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE CODESPACES GITPOD_WORKSPACE_ID SSH_CONNECTION DISPLAY WAYLAND_DISPLAY; do
  if [ -n "$(printenv "$name")" ]; then echo "set: $name"; fi
done
if [ -f /.dockerenv ] || [ -f /run/.containerenv ]; then echo "in a container"; fi
```

- `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE` (Claude Code's cloud sessions: on the web, in the desktop and mobile apps, and
  `claude --cloud`): a **hosted cloud session**. The person's browser can't open anything on its loopback, nothing
  forwards a port from it, and whatever is installed here is gone when the session ends.
- Linux in a container, with no `DISPLAY` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` and none of the signals below (a Codex cloud task
  looks like this): most likely a hosted sandbox too. Treat it as one.
- `CODESPACES`, `GITPOD_WORKSPACE_ID` (GitHub Codespaces, Ona) or `SSH_CONNECTION`: a remote machine. **This
  computer** works only through its port forward, or a tunnel they already use (`ssh -L`).
- macOS, or Linux with a display and none of the above: their own computer.

In a hosted cloud session or sandbox, say so first, in one or two sentences, before the questions below: AgentRun
installed here could not be opened from their browser, and its data and keys would vanish with the session.

## 2. Ask where it runs, and whether to look for their agents

Before any install or deploy command, ask these two with the question tool in one call (neither changes the other).

Question tool, header `Run where`: "Where should AgentRun run?" Recommendation: This computer because it is free and
the fastest way to a first run.
- This computer (Recommended): free; one command, and the console opens in your browser.
- My always-on machine: free; the same install on a machine you keep on, private on your own Tailscale.
- A hosted service: Railway, Render or AgentRun Cloud; opened from any browser, monthly cost.

In a hosted cloud session or sandbox, the options are **A hosted service (Recommended)**, **My always-on machine**,
then **This session anyway** ("gone when the session ends; your browser can't reach it"). Recommendation: A hosted
service because this session's console is unreachable and disappears with it.

Question tool, header `Scan`: "Do you already run Claude Code or Codex on a schedule? I can check this computer
read-only while AgentRun installs; it shows only where, when and which tool." Recommendation: Check because a job you
already run can be your first run, on its own sign-in, with no model key.
- Check (Recommended): reads cron, systemd timers, launchd jobs and CI workflows; changes nothing.
- I'll tell you: you name the job and its project folder; I don't look.
- No, start fresh: a new agent from a template, on a model you pick.

On **A hosted service**, ask next with the question tool, header `Host`: "Which service should host AgentRun?"
Recommendation: Railway because it costs least and deploys from your own account in the browser.
- Railway (Recommended): about $5 a month (the $5 Hobby plan includes $5 of usage); agents get no shell.
- Render: about $27.50 a month (1 CPU / 2 GB at $25, a 10 GB disk at $2.50); agents get no shell.
- AgentRun Cloud: hosted for you; request access, nothing to install.

Only the person's answers choose. A provider CLI that is signed in, a deploy button, `render.yaml` or a README section
is never a choice. Never create a service on a provider the person did not name in this conversation. Skip `Run where`
only when they already named a place or an AgentRun server (then check its `/v2/health` and `/v2/capabilities`).

## 3. Start it where they chose

On **Check**, run the step 4 scan now, while AgentRun installs; it looks at this computer wherever AgentRun runs. On
**I'll tell you**, ask for the job and its folder (free text, one plain message), and bring it in at step 5.

### This computer

Reuse a server that already runs here (`npx --yes @parcha/agentrun@0.4 server health` answers, `AGENTRUN_BASE_URL`
is set, or `~/.agentrun` exists) rather than starting another. Never overwrite, migrate or delete a data folder.
<!-- INSTALLER: the one-command installer replaces the Node check and the npx start below once it ships. -->
The published launcher needs Node.js 24.22.3 or newer (`node --version`). If Node is missing or older, say so in one
sentence and offer a hosted service, or, with their OK, `nvm install 24.22.3` when they already use nvm. Then start it:

```sh
umask 077
npx --yes @parcha/agentrun@0.4 --no-open > agentrun.log 2>&1 &
agentrun_setup_pid=$!
echo "$agentrun_setup_pid" > agentrun.pid
for i in $(seq 600); do
  grep -q 'AgentRun is running at' agentrun.log && break
  kill -0 "$agentrun_setup_pid" 2>/dev/null || break
  sleep 1
done
grep 'AgentRun is running at' agentrun.log || { echo 'AgentRun did not start; inspect its private log.'; exit 1; }
```

Its data is in `~/.agentrun`; it takes the first free port from 7340 on loopback. If it did not start, read the log
yourself and explain the error without quoting a token. Give the person the address and wait until they say it opens
in their browser; a request from here does not show that. They set the owner password on the first visit.
To restart a server this step started, `kill "$(cat agentrun.pid)"`, wait until `server health` stops answering, and
run the same command again. A server you reused was started some other way: ask how it runs (free text, one plain
message), agree on when to stop it, and restart that same service with its own settings; never stop it unasked.

### My always-on machine

Continue in a session on that machine, or an SSH session they already use. With their OK, run
`curl -fsSL https://agentrun.ai/install | sh -s -- --tailscale`: it installs AgentRun as a service, shares it on their
own tailnet only (`tailscale serve`, never Funnel) and prints its `https://<machine>.<tailnet DNS name>/` address. When
Tailscale is missing or signed out, or Linux needs operator rights, it prints the steps and the command to run again;
pass them on, and never run `sudo` or `tailscale up` for them. It asks for a setup code (below).

### A hosted service

<!-- RAILWAY: the template's deploy button replaces the Railway steps once it is published. -->
- **Railway:** the person deploys it from their own Railway account, in their browser: a new service from the image
  `ghcr.io/parcha-ai/agentrun-server:beta`, a volume at `/data`, a public domain, and the variables `PORT=7340` and
  `AGENTRUN_PUBLIC_URL=https://${{RAILWAY_PUBLIC_DOMAIN}}`. Leave `AGENTRUN_SEAL_KEY` unset; the server keeps its own
  key on the volume. Walk them through it; never create the service yourself with a Railway CLI.
- **Render:** they open https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/Parcha-ai/agentrun and confirm the plan
  Render shows; it reads the repository's `render.yaml` (the published image, 1 CPU / 2 GB, a 10 GB disk).
- **AgentRun Cloud:** hosted for you, by request. They request access at https://console.agentrun.ai/ and follow its
  onboarding; the steps below don't apply. For team onboarding, offer https://calendly.com/d/dtwn-dsp-nx5/agentrun.

### The setup code

A server at a public address asks for a **setup code** before the first password; say where it is with the address.
On Render, the **Environment** tab holds `AGENTRUN_TOKEN`; they paste its value into **Setup code**. Elsewhere, the
server's log has `Set up this server: <address>/setup#code=<code>`: read it privately and give them the newest such
link. Never put the API token (`AGENTRUN_TOKEN`, or `.token` in the data folder) in the chat. The link works **once**
and **expires 30 minutes** after it was printed. Then they press **Get a new code**, or you send
`curl -sS -X POST "$CONSOLE_ADDRESS/v2/setup/code"` (it never returns the code) and read the newest line. A server
that answers that with 404 has no such button: restarting it prints a new code.

## 4. Look for the agents they already run

On **Check**, run this as written. It reads cron, systemd timers (the system's and the person's own), launchd jobs and
the project's CI workflows, and reads the command each one runs, because a list of timers or launchd labels alone does
not show it.

Docker Compose

This guide will walk you through deploying Langfuse locally or on a VM using Docker Compose. We will use the docker-compose.yml file. This is the simplest way to run Langfuse to give it a try.

If you would rather not run any infrastructure, use Langfuse Cloud: hosted by Langfuse, with a free tier and no infrastructure to run. The SDKs and integrations work identically against Langfuse Cloud and a self-hosted instance.

If you use a cloud provider like AWS, GCP, or Azure, you will need permissions to deploy virtual machines.

For high-availability and high-throughput, we recommend using Kubernetes (deployment guide). The docker compose setup lacks high-availability, scaling capabilities, and backup functionality.

Coming from docker-compose v2? See our upgrade guide for docker compose.

Walkthrough

Watch this 2:15 minute walkthrough for a step-by-step guide on running Langfuse locally with Docker Compose.

Get Started
Local
VM
Requirements
git
docker & docker compose -> use Docker Desktop on Mac or Windows

On Apple silicon, you can also run Langfuse locally with Apple’s container runtime.

Clone Langfuse Repository

Get a copy of the latest Langfuse repository:

git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git
cd langfuse
Start the application

Update the secrets in the docker-compose.yml and then run the langfuse docker compose using:

docker compose up

Watch the containers being started and the logs flowing in. After about 2-3 minutes, the langfuse-web-1 container should log "Ready". At this point you can proceed to the next step.

Done

And you are ready to go! Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser to access the Langfuse UI.

There is no default login. Langfuse does not ship with a built-in admin account or password. Click Sign up on the login page to create the first user, then create your organization and project in the UI. To pre-create the organization, project, API keys, and first user without the UI, use headless initialization.

Docker log rotation

The default docker-compose.yml inherits the Docker daemon's logging configuration. Docker's default json-file driver does not rotate logs unless configured, which can exhaust disk space. Set its max-size and max-file options, or keep your chosen logging backend and configure retention there. Do not rotate or truncate Docker-managed JSON log files with external tools.

After changing daemon logging defaults, restart Docker and recreate existing containers to apply them; restarting containers alone is insufficient. Plan for interruption and preserve data volumes. These settings cover container stdout/stderr, not database data volumes or ClickHouse's internal log files.

AI Gateway

The default docker-compose.yml includes the AI Gateway (beta) as the langfuse-ai-gateway service, listening on port 3031. It needs Langfuse newer than v4.75.0; LANGFUSE_IMAGE_TAG sets the tag of web, worker, and gateway together. The gateway stays idle, with 503 on /ready, until you add its two keys to .env:

# Start on a new line if .env doesn't end with one.
[ -n "$(tail -c1 .env 2>/dev/null)" ] && echo >> .env
echo "LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_SERVICE_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)" >> .env
printf '%s\n' "LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_JWT_PRIVATE_KEY='$(openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout | awk '{printf "%s\\n", $0}')'" >> .env
docker compose up -d --pull always

Web shows http://localhost:3031 as the gateway's public URL, which only works on the Docker host. On a remote host, or whenever users reach Langfuse from other machines, set LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_URL in .env to the address clients use, and put a TLS-terminating reverse proxy in front of the gateway.

If you build web yourself, for example for a custom base path, rebuild it from a supported release and omit --pull always, which would replace your image. For TLS, other settings, and key rotation, see the AI Gateway guide.

Features

Langfuse supports many configuration options and self-hosted features. For more details, please refer to the configuration guide.

AI Gateway (beta)
Authentication & SSO
Automated Access Provisioning
Caching
Code evaluators
Halo
Custom Base Path
Encryption
Headless Initialization
Data Masking
Networking
Organization Creators (EE)
Instance Management API (EE)
Health and Readiness Check
Observability via OpenTelemetry
Transactional Emails
UI Customization (EE)
Scaling

Docker compose does not support horizontal scaling without an additional Load Balancer component. We recommend to use one of the other deployment options if your load exceeds single-instance scale or requires high availability. To add more throughput on a docker compose setup, you can usually use a larger virtual machine, i.e. scale vertically.

Shutdown

You can stop the containers by hitting Ctrl+C in the terminal. If you started docker-compose in the background (-d flag), you can stop all instance using:

docker compose down

Adding the -v flag will also remove the volumes.

Ensure to stop the VM instance in your cloud provider interface to avoid unnecessary costs.

Changing the exposed ports

The default docker-compose.yml publishes two services on the host: the Langfuse UI on port 3000 (langfuse-web, mapping 3000:3000) and MinIO on port 9090 (mapping 9090:9000). If one of these ports is already taken on your machine, change the host side of the mapping (the left value) and leave the container side unchanged, for example 3001:3000 for the UI.

When you change a port, also update the URLs that point at it:

NEXTAUTH_URL must match the URL users open in the browser, for example http://localhost:3001. Langfuse uses it for authentication callbacks and for links in the UI and in emails.
LANGFUSE_S3_MEDIA_UPLOAD_ENDPOINT on langfuse-web defaults to http://localhost:9090 and must point at the new MinIO host port, because browsers upload and download media through this URL.
The AI Gateway publishes port 3031. To change it, set LANGFUSE_AI_GATEWAY_PORT in .env; its port mapping and default public URL follow it.

Ports that are bound to 127.0.0.1 (the worker on 3030, MinIO console on 9091, and the databases) are only reachable from the host itself and usually do not need to change.

Troubleshooting
Multimodal tracing is not working: This docker compose setup by default uses MinIO for blob storage which is not accessible from outside the Docker network for direct uploads. Please refer to the blob storage guide for more details on how to configure MinIO for media uploads.
Make sure that the VM has enough disk space for accumulating traces.
How to Upgrade

To upgrade Langfuse, you can stop the containers and run docker compose up --pull always.

For more details on upgrading, please refer to the upgrade guide.

If you experience any issues when self-hosting Langfuse, please:

Check out Troubleshooting & FAQ page.
Use Ask AI to get instant answers to your questions.
Ask the maintainers on GitHub Discussions.
Create a bug report or feature request on GitHub.

OpenTelemetry (OTEL) for LLM Observability

OpenTelemetry (OTEL) is a CNCF project that provides a set of specifications, APIs, and libraries that define a standard way to collect distributed traces and metrics from your application.

Use this page if your application, framework, or collector already emits OpenTelemetry (OTEL) traces and you want to send them to Langfuse.

Using Python or JavaScript/TypeScript? Use the Langfuse SDK instead of building directly on the OTEL API. The SDK handles Langfuse attributes, propagation, media, filtering, and export for you. For other languages, use the native OpenTelemetry API for your language and export spans to Langfuse.

OpenTelemetry endpoint

Langfuse can receive traces on the /api/public/otel (OTLP) endpoint.

If you use a Collector that uses the OpenTelemetry SDK to export traces, you can use the following configuration:

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel" # 🇪🇺 EU data region
# Other Langfuse data regions include 🇺🇸 US: https://us.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel, 🇯🇵 Japan: https://jp.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel and ⚕️ HIPAA: https://hipaa.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel
# OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="http://localhost:3000/api/public/otel" # 🏠 Local deployment (>= v3.22.0)
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Basic ${AUTH_STRING},x-langfuse-ingestion-version=4"

Langfuse uses Basic Auth to authenticate requests.

You can use the following command to get the base64 encoded API keys (referred to as AUTH_STRING): echo -n "pk-lf-1234567890:sk-lf-1234567890" | base64. For long API Keys on GNU systems, you may have to add -w 0 at the end since base64 auto-wraps columns.

Enable real-time ingestion in Langfuse v4

If you send spans directly via OpenTelemetry, include the x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4 header so that new data appears in real time on the v4 data model and the v2 Observations and Metrics APIs. Without this header, directly ingested OpenTelemetry data can be delayed by up to 10 minutes. The OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS configuration above already includes the header.

If your setup uses signal-specific header settings, configure the same header on the traces exporter:

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_HEADERS="Authorization=Basic ${AUTH_STRING},x-langfuse-ingestion-version=4"

If your collector requires signal-specific environment variables, the trace endpoint is /api/public/otel/v1/traces.

OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT="https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel/v1/traces" # EU data region
# Other Langfuse data regions include 🇺🇸 US: https://us.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel/v1/traces, 🇯🇵 Japan: https://jp.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel/v1/traces and ⚕️ HIPAA: https://hipaa.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel/v1/traces

Please note that Langfuse currently supports OTLP over HTTP with both HTTP/JSON and HTTP/protobuf. gRPC is not supported yet.

Migrating to Langfuse v4? If you send custom events to the legacy /api/public/ingestion endpoint, or already send OTEL spans that rely on trace input/output or root-only attributes, follow the custom ingestion migration guide.

Langfuse can operate as an OpenTelemetry Backend to receive traces on the /api/public/otel (OTLP) endpoint. In addition to the Langfuse SDKs and native integrations, this OpenTelemetry endpoint is designed to increase compatibility with frameworks, libraries, and languages beyond the SDKs and native integrations. Popular OpenTelemetry libraries include OpenLLMetry and OpenLIT which extend Language support of Langfuse tracing to Java and Go and cover frameworks such as AutoGen, Semantic Kernel, and more.

As the Semantic Conventions for GenAI attributes on traces are still evolving, Langfuse maps the received OTel traces to the Langfuse data model and supports additional attributes that are popular in the OTel GenAI ecosystem (attribute mapping). Please contribute to the discussion on GitHub if an integration does not work as expected or does not parse the correct attributes.

Using other OTEL-based tools? If you're using Langfuse alongside other OpenTelemetry-based tools, you may run into conflicts. See Using Langfuse with an Existing OpenTelemetry Setup for configuration guidance.

Important: If you want to filter and aggregate by userId, sessionId, metadata, version, release, or tags, you need to propagate these trace-level attributes to every span in the trace. Start with Propagating Trace Attributes to All Spans before wiring this up in production.

OTLP replaces the deprecated POST /api/public/ingestion API. See Migration of deprecated APIs for the endpoint mapping; the deprecated endpoint itself is documented in its endpoint reference section.

Important: Propagating Trace Attributes to All Spans

When using OpenTelemetry (OTEL) instrumentation to send traces to Langfuse, certain trace-level attributes should be propagated to all spans within a trace to enable accurate aggregations and filtering in Langfuse. These attributes include:

userId (via langfuse.user.id or user.id)
sessionId (via langfuse.session.id or session.id)
metadata (via langfuse.trace.metadata.* for top-level metadata keys)
version (via langfuse.version)
release (via langfuse.release)
tags (via langfuse.trace.tags)
trace_name (via langfuse.trace.name)

Langfuse filters and aggregations increasingly operate across individual observations rather than only at the trace level. If you want to reliably filter or aggregate by these attributes, they need to be present on each span in the trace, not only on the root span.

Recommended: Use OpenTelemetry Baggage for Propagation

The recommended approach for propagating these attributes across all spans is to use OpenTelemetry Baggage with a BaggageSpanProcessor. Baggage is a built-in OpenTelemetry mechanism for context propagation that automatically copies specified key-value pairs to all spans within a trace context.

To implement this pattern:

Set the desired attributes as baggage entries at the beginning of your trace.
Set the attributes on the currently active span.
Configure a BaggageSpanProcessor in your OpenTelemetry setup to automatically copy baggage entries to span attributes.
The processor will ensure all downstream spans in the trace context receive these attributes.

For implementation details and code examples, refer to the OpenTelemetry documentation for Python and JavaScript.

Security Consideration: OpenTelemetry baggage is propagated across service boundaries and to third-party APIs. Do not include sensitive information (passwords, API keys, personal data, etc.) in baggage when using this approach, as it will be transmitted to all downstream services.

Alternative: Use Langfuse SDK Helpers

If you're using the Langfuse SDKs with OpenTelemetry integration, you can use the convenience methods propagate_attributes() (Python) or propagateAttributes() (TypeScript), which handle attribute propagation automatically. These methods provide a simpler interface and are the recommended approach when using Langfuse SDKs.

Ingestion Options
OpenTelemetry-native Langfuse SDKs

The quickest path to start tracing with Langfuse is the OTEL-native Langfuse SDK for Python or JS/TS. The SDK is a thin layer on top of the official OpenTelemetry client that automatically converts emitted spans into Langfuse observations (Langfuse calls spans observations; span is also a specific observation type) and adds first-class helpers for LLM-specific features such as token usage, cost tracking, prompt linking, and scoring.

Because it lives in the shared OpenTelemetry context, spans from other OTEL-instrumented libraries can be exported to Langfuse too. By default, Langfuse focuses on LLM-relevant spans (Langfuse SDK spans, spans with gen_ai.* attributes, and known LLM instrumentors). To export everything, use a permissive custom filter as described in the advanced SDK docs.

Get started by following the SDK overview.

Custom via OpenTelemetry SDKs

You can use the OpenTelemetry SDKs to directly export traces to Langfuse with the configuration mentioned above. Thereby, Language support of Langfuse is extended to other languages than the ones supported by the Langfuse SDKs (Python and JS/TS).

Run experiments via OpenTelemetry

To group direct-OTEL traces as Langfuse experiments, start with Experiments via OpenTelemetry and then add the experiment and item attributes described in Ingest experiment spans with OpenTelemetry.

Export from OpenTelemetry Collector

Application with OTel Instrumentation

OpenTelemetry Collector

Langfuse

If you run an OpenTelemetry Collector, you can use the following configuration to export traces to Langfuse:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
    grpc:
      endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
    http:
      endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
processors:
  batch:
  memory_limiter:
    # 80% of maximum memory up to 2G
    limit_mib: 1500
    # 25% of limit up to 2G
    spike_limit_mib: 512
    check_interval: 5s
exporters:
  otlphttp/langfuse:
    endpoint: "https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel" # EU data region
    # Other regions: US https://us.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel, Japan https://jp.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel, HIPAA https://hipaa.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel
    headers:
      Authorization: "Basic ${AUTH_STRING}" # Previously encoded API keys
      x-langfuse-ingestion-version: "4"
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/langfuse]
Filtering Spans sent to Langfuse

In case you want to selectively send OTel Spans to Langfuse, you can use the OTel Collector filterprocessor. It enables you to filter spans based on attributes, span names, and more. As this applies on a Span level, you may risk incomplete traces and should be careful when applying complex filter rules. Langfuse also requires that a root span is sent to our backend to ensure that a trace is created correctly.

With the configuration below, you would only forward Spans which have a gen_ai.system attribute set to openai:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
    grpc:
      endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
    http:
      endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
processors:
  filter/openaisystem:
    error_mode: ignore
    traces:
      span:
        - 'attributes["gen_ai.system"] != "openai"'
exporters:
  otlphttp/langfuse:
    endpoint: "https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel" # EU data region
    # Other regions: US https://us.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel, Japan https://jp.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel, HIPAA https://hipaa.cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel
    headers:
      Authorization: "Basic ${AUTH_STRING}" # Previously encoded API keys
      x-langfuse-ingestion-version: "4"
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [filter/openaisystem]
      exporter
